paras: The threatened lynching of Emmett Claud took place in Southampton County, Virginia, in late December 1881 and early January 1882, after two store clerks were murdered at Green Plains and false reports of lynchings spread through the press. Wire dispatches of December 27 said two suspects had been captured and hanged, and briefs in early January said Claud, a Black man accused of the murders, had been lynched by a mob. The Richmond Dispatch called the first report untrue and placed Claud alive in the county jail, awaiting the grand jury, as late as January 14.

On the night of December 23, 1881, clerks John Murrell, 21, and Thomas Glover, 16, were killed in the store of Joseph H. and J. B. Prince at Green Plains, which was robbed and burned with their bodies inside. Suspicion first fell on two white strangers thought to be sailors or tramps, and a Petersburg telegram predicted "summary justice" if they were caught.

On December 27 a Petersburg wire reported that the two men charged with the murders had been taken to the scene and "hanged to a tree"; a variant said they were taken from jail. The Dispatch's Petersburg correspondent answered that the reports were untrue "on information direct from the vicinity," that the strangers were now thought innocent, and that "negroes living in the county" were suspected.

After two white men arrested at Norfolk were discounted, J. H. Prince offered a $500 reward and summoned Detective Wren of Richmond. On the night of December 29 Wren arrested Claud, a "colored man" who lived half a mile from the store, at Hicksford, chiefly because he was said to have spent $63 there after the murders. A coroner's jury found that the clerks died at his hands, and Justice Hughes committed him to the jail at Jerusalem, the county seat, for indictment.

Wren reported "great indignation in the county" and "some probability of Claud being lynched." By January 3 Claud had asked for a guard around the jail for fear of a lynching; the coverage does not show whether one was posted.

A report that Claud had confessed, carried by the Petersburg Index-Appeal and the Alexandria Gazette, could not be traced to any reliable source, according to the Dispatch. In mid-January the Dispatch wrote that his case would go before the grand jury, that the evidence was wholly circumstantial, and that he had made no confession. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict was found.

The December lynching report ran on December 28 in the New-York Tribune as "Murderers Said to Have Been Lynched" and in the Savannah Morning News as "Virginia Murderers Lynched." The St. Paul Daily Globe, the Chicago Daily Tribune and the National Republican carried it the same day, and the Memphis Daily Appeal printed it in its crime column, "Our Black Book." The texts kept the hedge "it is reported," but the headlines presented the hanging as fact and called the uncaught suspects "murderers."

In January digest columns stated Claud's lynching without qualification. The Maysville Daily Evening Bulletin placed it at "Belleville, Ky." with a mob of two hundred, Michigan's Crawford Avalanche credited fifty masked men, and the Huntsville Gazette and Grenada Sentinel reprinted a brief calling him "a negro."

The Richmond Dispatch, drawing on a Petersburg correspondent, denied the first report and followed Claud's confinement. It called the case "the Southampton horror," referred to Claud as "the negro" or "colored," and doubted the confession report.

The December lynching rested on a rumor the Dispatch said was untrue, and the January briefs disagree on place and mob size and conflict with Dispatch reports from January 3 to 14 placing Claud in jail. The Dispatch reports came from correspondents near the scene and continued after the briefs, tracing the case toward the grand jury.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Emmett Claud
bases: The episode consists of wire reports that suspects in the Green Plains murders were lynched (A4, A18) and of reported threats to lynch the accused Emmett Claud in jail (A17, A19); no killing is confirmed by local reports (A10, A27).

The December report that two suspects were hanged was called untrue by the Dispatch's Petersburg correspondent (A10), and the January briefs that Claud was lynched by a mob (A18, A20, A26) are contradicted by Dispatch reports placing him alive in the Southampton jail through January 14 (A19, A23, A27); what the local coverage shows is a threat, tied to the murder accusation (A17, A19).
Wire and digest briefs reported lynchings (A4, A11, A18, A26), while the Richmond Dispatch denied the first report and later placed Claud in jail awaiting the grand jury (A10, A19, A27).

framing.detail: Papers from New York to Savannah ran the Petersburg rumor under headlines such as 'Murderers Lynched', calling the uncaught suspects 'murderers'.
The Richmond Dispatch denied the lynching report, called the case 'the Southampton horror', referred to Claud as 'the negro' and 'colored', and stressed that the evidence was circumstantial.
January digest columns stated Claud's lynching as fact, without hedging, as one item among unrelated crimes.
